entry.title: Inside PIXBOOM – Factory Tour of the “Spark” High-Speed Camera in China
entry.summary: Recently, I packed my bag in Japan and flew to Shenzhen, China to visit PIXBOOM, the young company behind the Spark high-speed camera. I visited the factory in Dongguan, where the camera is assembled and tested, and learned about a new production line that will start operating so
entry.content:
Recently, I packed my bag in Japan and flew to Shenzhen, China to visit PIXBOOM, the young company behind the Spark high-speed camera. I visited the factory in Dongguan, where the camera is assembled and tested, and learned about a new production line that will start operating soon. I was also kindly invited to see the unique office in Shenzhen and meet the people behind this company. Here is my report, guys, and I hope you enjoy the journey as much as I did.

My trip started at Osaka’s Kansai Airport. Shenzhen has become one of the most important places in the world for technology and electronics manufacturing, and it is also home to PIXBOOM. By now, I am sure most of you know the company by now, its first camera being the PIXBOOM Spark, a compact Super 35 high-speed camera with a backside-illuminated (BSI) global shutter sensor, up to 1,000 fps in 4K and continuous RAW recording to a removable SSD. The idea behind it is simple: bring extreme slow motion to filmmakers who could never justify renting a traditional high-speed package. I wanted to meet the people behind this idea, and see how the camera is actually made.

We at CineD have been covering the Spark’s journey from the very beginning. We reported about the Kickstarter launch at IBC 2025, where the camera also won a CineD Best-of-Show Award. We then took a beta unit to India for our first hands-on review, and my colleague Gunther shot a wildlife documentary in Goa with it. Later we reported on the first production unit, the start of shipping in May, and the latest firmware updates. But we wanted to go deeper, and so we decided to see where the camera is born – the factory floor.

From a research lab to a Kickstarter success

The PIXBOOM company story started in a research lab. Its co-founders, Dr. Huang and Dr. Chengyang, were PhD students working on ultra-high-speed imaging systems for scientific use, capable of capturing millions of frames per second. In 2015, they set out to make high-speed imaging accessible to a much wider group of creators, and over the years they moved from lab experiments to real-world prototypes, refined with feedback from filmmakers. You can read the company’s own account of that journey on its Spark history page.

The camera made quite an impression before it even reached the market. During its Kickstarter campaign, PIXBOOM raised around $3.5 million, and to be honest, it is not hard to see why.

Why is the factory in Dongguan?

My first question was a practical one: why is the factory so far from the center of town? The answer was very straightforward: Shenzhen is often called China’s Silicon Valley, but the manufacturing usually happens in the neighboring city of Dongguan. “Everybody just knows the good factories are usually based in Dongguan,” I was told. So off we went. After meeting the core team in the factory offices, I finally saw the place where the Spark is made.

Quality control for a camera that runs hot

A high-speed camera pushes a huge amount of data through its electronics, so I was curious how quality control works here. The team explained that the Spark goes through the usual checks of any electronic product: basic signals, image quality, calibration, and sensor adjustments. “But for high speed, one important point is the cooling.” Every camera goes through a strict high-temperature test in the factory, running continuously in a heat chamber for cycles of several hours. “If it survives this test, it can be shipped.”

The Spark uses active cooling with intake and exhaust vents, and PIXBOOM rates it for operation between 0°C and 40°C (32°F to 104°F). A camera designed to be rigged on cars, robotic arms, and gimbals has to keep working, even under direct sunlight. These heat tests ensure that it can handle these conditions before it leaves the building.

What does a BSI sensor do for slow motion?

I asked the team to explain why they decided on a BSI sensor. BSI stands for backside illumination. It is a semiconductor process that flips the wafer, so light reaches the photodiode from the back side, and this improves the light efficiency of each pixel. “For high-speed video or slow motion, one important issue is the light demand,” I was told. “BSI improves the light efficiency to get brighter footage under the same lighting conditions.”

Anyone who has ever shot at 1,000 fps knows the problem: every frame gets only a tiny slice of exposure time, so light is always the first thing that runs out. The company says the Spark needs only about 25% of the light a typical high-speed setup calls for, and that the BSI design increases quantum efficiency from around 60% to more than 80%. For slow motion in real locations, every bit of extra sensitivity counts.

The compromises of a first camera

Going from concept to finished product is a long journey, and the final result often looks what a little different from what you originally had in mind. So, I asked whether the team had to compromise anywhere, and the answer was honest. “Because we are a start-up company and Spark is our first camera, we need to focus on the main mission of this camera, which is to bring a good slow-motion camera to our creators”, I was told by Dr. Huang.

That means no audio and no autofocus. Autofocus is relatively complex, and according to the team, feedback from users also played a role in that decision. On audio, the explanation was clear: “To add audio into Spark is easy. But to make it fully usable and 100% perfect is difficult. Audio is a very deep and large field.” In my opinion, as a documentary shooter who always records sound, this is a decision that some people will miss. (The camera can shoot at 24/25 fps too.) At the same time, slow-motion footage is very rarely used with its original sound, and a focused product is often a better first product. I’ll let you guys decide for yourselves, as everyone works a bit differently.

An empty hall that will soon be busy

When I asked where the company sees itself in three years, and whether PIXBOOM will still be making only one camera, the answer was short: “We will have more…”

Then Dr. Huang, PIXBOOM’s CTO, showed me a large, empty hall. “It’s empty now, but it will be very busy in one or two months,” he said. “This is a new factory line for our PIXBOOM camera. We are trying to get people, devices, and instruments here to build a new line for the Spark camera.” Looking at the empty workstations, it was easy to imagine how this space would look when it is full of workers and products.

Back in Shenzhen: the people behind the product

After a quick lunch, we drove back to Shenzhen, a city of nearly 18 million people that has grown from a small fishing town into one of China’s leading tech hubs in just a few decades. Skyscrapers, busy highways, and technology are everywhere you look. The PIXBOOM offices, however, are a very unique space.

I asked Jing Qi, PIXBOOM’s Chief Marketing Officer, about the concept behind the space. At the beginning, she said, the team was very small, and everyone had to do multiple jobs to get the company off the ground. “But at the same time, we need to consider how to make people comfortable, so they enjoy staying and working here,” she explained. “It’s a space where we spend more than eight hours a day.” Jing doesn’t see herself in the classic marketing role. “I treat myself like a bridge,” she told me, “between the company and filmmakers, between me and my team, and between cultures. So my role is to break the boundaries.”

Spark specs at a glance

For those of you who don’t know the Spark camera, here is a short summary: It uses a 14.2MP Super 35 global shutter BSI CMOS sensor (25.34 x 16.90mm) with 4.6K 3:2 open gate resolution (4608 x 3072), dual native ISO with settings from 400 to 1600, and 13 stops of dynamic range, according to PIXBOOM. Top frame rates in PIXBOOM RAW are 670 fps at 4.6K open gate, 887 fps at 4K 16:9, and 2,182 fps at 2K 2.37:1, with custom resolutions that go higher still. The camera currently records 10-bit RAW, and 12-bit RAW is in development.

Recording goes to the removable 2.5TB PIXBOOM Pro Card at up to 10GB/s, so record time is limited only by card capacity. The card offloads directly via USB-C at 20Gbps, without a card reader. The all-aluminum body weighs about 1.1kg (2.42lb) and measures 108 x 110 x 130mm (4.25 x 4.33 x 5.12in). It integrates a 3.5-inch 6.22M-dot touchscreen, a V-Lock battery plate, 12G-SDI and HDMI 2.0 outputs (both 4K 60p), a 9-pin EXT port, and Wi-Fi control. Interchangeable locking adapters are available for E, EF, and PL mount. Genlock, timecode, and some remote features are still under development and will need future firmware or the upcoming I/O expansion accessory.

Price and availability

The PIXBOOM Spark is shipping now. The package includes the camera body, a 2.5TB PIXBOOM Pro Card, and one mount adapter (E, EF, or PL), in silver or black. B&H lists it at $13,999, and CVP lists it at €12,749.95 (excluding VAT). Additional mount adapters cost $599 each, and an extra 2.5TB Pro Card costs $2,999. Retailer stock varies by mount and color, so check the listing for your configuration.

PIXBOOM is still early in its journey, but that is exactly what makes it so interesting. What I saw was a young company with big ambitions and a lot of energy, trying to carve out its own place in the world of cinema cameras. I am curious to see where they go from here.

Many thanks to: Dr. Huang, CTO; Chengyang Hu, Founder and CEO; Jing Qi, Chief Marketing Officer; Xin Tang, Supply Chain Director; Wong Haoyuan, Head of Visual Design; Max Zhai, Head of R&D; Daisy Wu, Senior Project Manager; Vicky Wen, Head of Customer Service Center; Ariel Levesque, PIXBOOM Spark footage; Little Beauty, Chief Pet Officer; and the entire PIXBOOM team!

What do you think about the PIXBOOM Spark and the idea of owning a high-speed camera instead of renting one? Would audio or autofocus matter to you in a camera like this? Please share your thoughts with us in the comment section below!

entry.title: Nikon ZR Firmware 2.00 Detailed – Log3G10 in H.265, Selectable High ISO NR and 3D LUT over HDMI
entry.summary: Nikon has published the full feature list of firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, the first major update for its RED-developed full-frame cinema camera. The update brings Log3G10 and REDWideGamutRGB to H.265 recording, a selectable High ISO NR level, more assignable controls,
entry.content:
Nikon has published the full feature list of firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, the first major update for its RED-developed full-frame cinema camera. The update brings Log3G10 and REDWideGamutRGB to H.265 recording, a selectable High ISO NR level, more assignable controls, focus peaking with a LUT applied in R3D NE, 3D LUT output over HDMI, and a fix for black-level flicker in low light. Nikon says the firmware is scheduled to be available before the end of the year, but it still gives no exact date.

The Nikon ZR has been on the market since October 2025, and its firmware history so far is short. Version 1.10 arrived in January 2026 with wired timecode sync, RED file naming and more, and version 1.11 in March fixed two bugs. In August, we reported that Nikon ZR owners were still waiting for a big firmware update, and in September, Nikon made the development announcement for firmware V2.00 with three confirmed features. The announcement of November 3 adds several items to that list. Let’s take a look at what it includes.

RED color science in a smaller file

The main change is a new tone mode option for H.265 recording. Until now, Log3G10 was not available for H.265 recording. With firmware 2.00, Log3G10 gamma and the REDWideGamutRGB color gamut are also available when the camera records H.265. According to Nikon, this gives footage in the compact H.265 format “the high color-grading latitude made possible by RED color science, with its smooth tonal gradation and exceptionally wide color gamut.”

For productions that do not need RAW on every shot, this means one Log3G10 color pipeline for both R3D NE and H.265 material, with much smaller files from the second. LUTs built for Log3G10, such as the Phantom LUTs for the Nikon ZR, target the same curve. H.265 on the ZR stays a 10-bit 4:2:0 codec, and Nikon has not said whether the update changes its processing.

Four levels of High ISO NR

The second feature from the development announcement is a selectable [High ISO NR] level. Nikon lists four settings, available when the camera records H.265 with Log3G10 or N-Log. The company describes the range as going “from shooting that prioritizes inherent textures to shooting that calls for smooth rendering with minimal noise.” Nikon gives no further details on what each level does. In September, we noted that this setting matches how the Nikon Z6III already handles high ISO noise reduction in H.265.

Another image processing change was not in the September announcement. Nikon says new processing “suppresses frame-by-frame fluctuations in black level, reducing flicker that tends to occur in low-light conditions and in dark areas of the frame.” The press release does not say which recording formats this applies to.

More assignable controls

Firmware 2.00 also extends the customization options. ISO sensitivity, exposure settings, white balance (WB) and white balance color temperature (WBK) can now be assigned to the command dials. In addition, [3D LUT/View Assist] can be assigned to an Fn button, so the operator can switch between the two with one press. Nikon’s position is that these changes let the operator adjust settings “without taking their eyes off the monitor.”

Monitoring: focus peaking in R3D NE and LUTs over HDMI

The third feature from September is focus peaking during R3D NE recording. The missing focus peaking in R3D NE was one of the most frequent owner complaints we listed in August, and one of the gaps that reviewers, us included in our Nikon ZR review, pointed out at launch. In the final wording, Nikon says focus peaking is now supported “even when a 3D LUT is applied during recording in R3D NE format.”

The ZR can also apply a 3D LUT to its HDMI video output. This lets an external monitor or a director’s monitor show a rendering close to the graded image, without loading the LUT on the monitor itself. The camera has a micro-HDMI port, and accessories such as the SmallRig micro-HDMI to HDMI adapter are made to protect that connection on a rig.

What is still missing

Open Gate recording and a desqueeze display for anamorphic lenses are not part of firmware 2.00. In its September announcement, Nikon said it is developing both features “with the goal of incorporating them in ZR firmware in 2027.” Several other requests from owners are also not in the November list, among them internal false color, an exposure meter in R3D NE, more compressed R3D NE options, and a lighter 10-bit 4:2:2 codec than ProRes 422 HQ. Third-party tools such as the ZR CTL control app continue to fill some of these gaps. In September, Nikon also said that RED is updating its RED CONTROL and RED CONTROL PRO apps to support the ZR.

Price and availability

Nikon says firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR is “scheduled to be available before the end of the year,” with no exact release date. The Nikon ZR body is available at B&H for $2,196.95 and at CVP for €1,804.69.

Are you a Nikon ZR owner, and which of these features will you use first? Is Log3G10 in H.265 enough for you, or are you waiting for Open Gate in 2027? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: DJI Osmo Pocket 4P Firmware V01.02.1149 Released – 18x Zoom, Smoother Lens Switching and Scene Presets
entry.summary: DJI has released firmware V01.02.1149 for the Osmo Pocket 4P, and it is the biggest update the dual-camera pocket gimbal has received so far. The roughly 1.1GB download raises the maximum zoom from 12x to 18x, improves ActiveTrack and the 60mm telephoto camera, adds Stage and Sun
entry.content:
DJI has released firmware V01.02.1149 for the Osmo Pocket 4P, and it is the biggest update the dual-camera pocket gimbal has received so far. The roughly 1.1GB download raises the maximum zoom from 12x to 18x, improves ActiveTrack and the 60mm telephoto camera, adds Stage and Sunset scene presets, and promises smoother transitions between the two cameras. That last point is the one I was waiting for, because it targets the exposure jump at 3x. First owner reports say it is better now, but not fixed for everyone.

The Osmo Pocket 4P is a camera that our team has spent a lot of time with. It pairs a 20mm-equivalent f/2.0 wide camera on a 1-inch LOFIC sensor with a 60mm-equivalent f/1.8 medium telephoto camera on a 1/1.28-inch sensor. We reported on the European launch of the Osmo Pocket 4P in July, and in our DJI Osmo Pocket 4P Lab Test (yes, that is my face in the latitude shots), the wide camera measured 16 stops of dynamic range at SNR = 2, the best result we have ever recorded. In August, DJI added cloud uploads and D-Log for slow motion. The new firmware goes much further. Let’s look at what it brings.

18x zoom, but only 3x is optical

The headline number is the new maximum zoom in photo and video modes: 18x instead of 12x, which is approximately 360mm in full-frame terms. Let’s be clear about what that means. Only the step from the 20mm wide camera to the 60mm telephoto camera is optical, and that gives you 3x. Everything above 3x is a crop of the telephoto sensor and, at the higher factors, an upscale of a small part of it. I would not expect 18x to give usable images for professional work, and my guess is that DJI added it mainly for the spec sheet and for social media clips.

The zoom changes that matter more to me are less visible. DJI says the telephoto camera now gives better image quality and sharpness in 4K/30p, and that zooming is smoother. Owners have already noticed one side effect: a long press on the zoom button now runs all the way to 18x, and there is no setting to stop it at a chosen factor. (DJI, a zoom limit in the menu would be a small change with a big effect. Please add it in the next update.)

The exposure jump at 3x: partly fixed

According to the changelog, transitions between the two camera modules during a zoom should now look more natural. This is the fix many Osmo Pocket 4P owners asked for. Since launch, the camera has shown a clear jump in brightness when it switches from the wide to the telephoto camera. That is not a big surprise, because the two cameras are different systems. In our lab test, the wide camera recorded D-Log 2 at a native ISO of 1600, and the telephoto camera recorded D-Log at a native ISO of 400.

First user reports on Reddit and Facebook are mixed. Several owners say that the jump in D-Log is gone, but only at ISO 400, the lowest ISO of the telephoto camera. Others say the jump is now approximately 1/3 stop, compared to one to two stops before. Some still see a visible change in brightness. My feeling is that DJI has improved the exposure match at specific settings, and not across the full ISO range. That is only my guess, though, so if a seamless zoom through 3x is important for your shoot, test it before you rely on it.

More ISO range in D-Log, according to users

Some changes are not in the official list. Several owners report that D-Log now starts at ISO 100 instead of ISO 400. D-Log 2 seems to get an Auto ISO option with a selectable range for the first time, but that range starts at ISO 400. DJI has not confirmed this. A lower ISO in D-Log is useful in bright sun when you do not have ND filters with you. Keep in mind that our lab results are for the native ISO settings, so we cannot yet say what ISO 100 does to the dynamic range of the telephoto camera.

Tracking, HDR and live output

DJI has also improved the performance and stability of ActiveTrack, the tracking function in which the gimbal keeps a selected subject in the frame. According to the release notes, the update also gives:

  • Steadier gimbal stabilization
  • Better image quality for Wi-Fi livestreams, the DisplayPort output and webcam mode
  • Better results in HDR scenes when portrait mode is off
  • Improved HDR playback on the camera screen

The livestream and webcam improvements show that DJI sees the Pocket 4P as more than a vlogging camera. It is also a small streaming and video call camera. DJI does not say how much the image quality of these outputs has changed, so I will not guess a number here.

Scene presets, Intelligent Highlight and file access

Two new scene presets, Stage and Sunset, adjust the camera settings automatically. A stage mode is also part of the Insta360 Luna Ultra firmware update with 15x zoom from September. I don’t think that is a coincidence: both companies now compete for concert footage, and both use long digital zoom ranges to do it. Intelligent Highlight finds highlight moments automatically during recording. Users can also mark highlights during playback and share them through the DJI Mimo app.

The other additions are about getting files off the camera:

  • Auto Media Transfer: photos and Live Photos can move to the smartphone automatically after capture.
  • Huawei Direct Transfer: owners of Huawei devices with HarmonyOS 6.1 or later can transfer footage from playback with one tap.
  • File access when off: the camera now connects by USB to a computer or an OTG-capable smartphone when it is switched off. In sleep mode, users can view and download footage through DJI Mimo.

For me, file access in the off state is the most practical change in this list. The camera no longer has to be switched on to show its 103GB of internal storage to a computer, which removes a small but frequent step at the end of every shoot day.

How to install the update

Firmware V01.02.1149 is free and available now through the DJI Mimo app. When we performed the update, we did not see it in the settings menu and could only find it on the start page of the app instead.

I also recommend a hard reset after the installation: hold the power button for 10 seconds to restart the camera.

DJI’s product and download pages are not available from the US, where the Osmo Pocket 4P is still not officially sold.

Price and availability

The Osmo Pocket 4P is available in Europe, the UK, Canada and Australia. DJI lists the Standard Combo at €599 and the Vlog Combo at €689, including VAT, on the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P product page. CVP lists the Standard Combo at €515.35 and the Vlog Combo at €588.98, excluding VAT. B&H does not list the camera, because it is not sold in the US.

Have you installed the new firmware on your Osmo Pocket 4P, and is the exposure jump at 3x gone on your camera? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: SmallRig x CineD OrBrella Crowdfunding Ends November 8 – Last Chance to Get the Campaign Price
entry.summary: Guys, this is the final week! The crowdfunding campaign for our SmallRig x CineD OrBrella soft light closes on November 8, 2026. After that, the 60W bi-color umbrella light will cost $80 more. So, if you were still on the fence about it, now is the last chance to grab it and save
entry.content:
Guys, this is the final week! The crowdfunding campaign for our SmallRig x CineD OrBrella soft light closes on November 8, 2026. After that, the 60W bi-color umbrella light will cost $80 more. So, if you were still on the fence about it, now is the last chance to grab it and save some money!

I can’t believe how fast these weeks went… It feels like yesterday that I stood at the SmallRig booth at IBC 2026 and watched all 200 early-bird units go in three days. The light also won a Future Best of Show Award at the show. If you missed the backstory, our launch article explains how the idea came about, and the crowdfunding article covers the IBC story and the full feature set. We also talked about it at length on Focus Check ep133. As the crowdfunding campaign is ending this week, I quickly wanted to remind you guys and also tell you why I think this light is useful. Keep reading to find out what you get if you back it before the campaign ends on November 8th.

Soft light in 15 seconds

For so long, my interview routine on documentary shoots was the same: put up a COB light, add a softbox, a grid, and a diffusion layer, and lose at least five minutes before the first question. The OrBrella turns this around. Eight LED strips sit on the ribs of a 58cm / 22.8 in umbrella and fire inward at the white fabric, so the source and the diffusion are one object. It opens in about five seconds, and in our comparison, the total setup takes around 15 seconds, against three to five minutes for a COB with a softbox.

On a face, the result is the wraparound, book-light quality that normally needs a bounce, a frame, and a stand for each. A supplied cap goes over the front if you want it even softer. Stefan Karle, CEO of DoPchoice, mentored me through the prototypes and helped us choose the diffusion fabric.

Two lights in one bag

When you need more punch, you press the knob at the end of a strip, pull it off its USB-C connector, and flip it so it faces forward. Each strip flips individually, so you can run half bounced and half direct. For me, this is the part I am proudest of, because it means one fixture in the bag instead of a soft light plus a harder key.

The OrBrella FM 60B is a 60W bi-color fixture with a range of 2,700 to 6,500K plus green/magenta correction. In my opinion, the green/magenta control matters most on location, where mixed fluorescent and daylight is exactly what a real room gives you. We chose 60W on purpose because we found it sufficient for sit-down indoor interviews.

Small, light, and flexible on power

Folded, the light is 34cm / 13.4in long and weighs 1.3kg / 2.87lb, so it fits in a camera bag next to a body and two lenses. Power runs through a separate control box on a permanently attached cable, so there is no cable to forget. The box takes a V-mount battery, USB-C from a power bank or laptop charger, or mains power. A Sony NP-F plate is available as an accessory. On a 99Wh V-mount battery, you get about 1.5 hours of runtime.

You control intensity, color temperature, and green/magenta on the box itself, or through the SmallRig app with NFC pairing. This way, you can trim the light from your chair while you set up the interview.

One honest reminder: the images you see here show a prototype. The light is still under development, and small details may change before the first batch ships.

Price and availability

Until November 8, 2026, the OrBrella FM 60B is $169.99 / €178.90 on SmallRig’s campaign page. Right after the campaign closes, the price goes up by $80. The reason is simple: the cost of components has gone up since we first set the retail price. The first batch is expected to ship on January 20, 2027. For more information, please visit our crowdfunding campaign here.

Before I close, a big thank you to the SmallRig team, to Stefan Karle (DoPchoice) for his patience and guidance, and to everyone who has already backed the light or stopped by the booth with feedback.

Will you find our light a place in your kit? Please share your thoughts with us in the comment section below!

entry.title: OFFBIT M1 Announced – E-Paper Display for Lens Charts, Crew Lists and Notes, Three-Week Battery
entry.summary: Barcelona-based startup OFFBIT has announced the M1, a small e-paper display for the camera department that replaces the paper lens chart on the camera body. It also holds the crew list, notes and a gallery of custom images, and everything is set up in a free iOS app. The first b
entry.content:
Barcelona-based startup OFFBIT has announced the M1, a small e-paper display for the camera department that replaces the paper lens chart on the camera body. It also holds the crew list, notes and a gallery of custom images, and everything is set up in a free iOS app. The first batch is limited to 100 units, and pre-orders open on November 11. Let’s take a look at what it offers.

Most camera departments still tape a printed lens chart to the camera or keep it in the AC’s pouch, next to a folded crew list and handwritten notes. The OFFBIT M1 puts that information on one small screen that mounts on the camera body or beside a monitor. OFFBIT founder Bernat Eguiluz, a working cinematographer, started the company in Barcelona in October 2025, and the M1 is its first product. According to OFFBIT, the M1 began as a prototype and was refined on productions with the help of focus pullers and 2nd ACs. Camera assistants are the main users.

E-paper is not new to filmmaking gear; we saw an E-Ink status screen on the Insta360 Mic Pro earlier this year. The M1 is, however, a dedicated reference display with no camera or recording function. It shows lens data, the crew list and notes, and the content comes from a free iPhone app over Bluetooth.

Three pages: lens, crew and notes

Three buttons along the top edge switch between the LENS, CREW and NOTES pages. OFFBIT’s press images show the LENS page as a grid of focal lengths, each with its T-stop and close-focus distance, plus the name of the lens set at the bottom. The CREW page lists names, roles and departments, and according to the OFFBIT website, the app can scan a call sheet to fill it in. NOTES is a free-form page for shot lists, radio channels or equipment lists, and the app can also scan a shooting plan into it.

A long press on the center button opens the patch gallery. It holds up to 25 custom images, such as production logos or crew photos. The app converts any image from the phone gallery to a bitmap and sends it to the M1, where the user switches between patches on the device itself. A fourth button on the left side handles pairing and settings.

Screen, housing and battery

The M1 has a 3.1-inch, 320 x 240 pixel black-and-white e-paper screen behind matte Gorilla Glass with an anti-reflective finish. According to the company, it stays readable in direct sunlight. The housing is CNC-machined from 6061 aluminum with a black anodized finish, and the device measures 85 x 60 x 10mm (3.35 x 2.36 x 0.39in) and weighs 71g (2.5oz). OFFBIT rates the 450mAh battery at up to three weeks on a single charge, and the M1 charges via USB-C. It connects to the phone over Bluetooth 5.0 LE.

Set up in the app, not on the device

All content is prepared in the free OFFBIT app and sent to the M1 over Bluetooth. The app includes a database of more than 2,500 lenses and supports custom lenses, which are stored locally. It does not need an account, and it works offline. According to OFFBIT, a connection is necessary only for app and firmware updates, and firmware updates are wireless and free. The company says a project takes minutes to build, and after that the device stays on the camera until something changes.

At launch, the app is available only for iOS on the App Store. An Android version is in development, but OFFBIT gives no release date. OFFBIT also states on its website that it does not sell user data and that there is no subscription.

Mounting and the M1 Backplate

The M1 has a flat back and attaches with Velcro. The box contains the device, eight Velcro loop strips and a welcome card. OFFBIT does not include a USB-C cable, and the website lists the charging input as 5V / 1A.

For camera bodies without a flat surface, OFFBIT offers the M1 Backplate (M1-BP) for €35. It is an aluminum plate with two 1/4″-20 threads and a locking 3/8″-16 point. The M1 attaches to the plate with Velcro, and the plate then mounts to a cage, a magic arm or a monitor.

“M1 saves prep time, but the real difference is on set: lenses, crew, notes and the shooting plan, all in one place. You stop looking for the paper that went missing,” says Bernat.

Current limitations

The M1 is a first product from a new company, and the first batch is small. The app is iOS only, so crews on Android phones cannot use the M1 yet. The screen is black and white at 320 x 240 pixels, which suits text and simple graphics, and patches are converted to a bitmap image. The three-week battery figure is a manufacturer claim. Shipping is limited to Spain and the rest of the EU at first, and the UK, the US and other markets are planned for spring 2027. OFFBIT has not announced US dollar or British pound prices.

Price and availability

The OFFBIT M1 costs €199 including VAT, and the M1 Backplate costs €35. Batch 01 is limited to 100 units, with a maximum of three per person. Pre-orders open on November 11, 2026, at 11:11 CET on the OFFBIT website, with full payment at checkout. Batch 01 ships to Spain and the rest of the EU in December 2026. At the time of writing, B&H and CVP do not list the M1. For more information, visit OFFBIT’s press page.

Would a small e-paper display replace the paper lens chart on your camera, or does tape and paper still do the job? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Instagram Pays Creators Up to $500,000 for Long-Form Features – 90-Minute Videos, TV App, No Ad Share Yet
entry.summary: Instagram is back in long-form video, and this time it brings a checkbook. The new Features format lets selected creators upload horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes, and according to an exclusive Business Insider report, Meta pays some creators between $50,000 and $500,000 to p
entry.content:
Instagram is back in long-form video, and this time it brings a checkbook. The new Features format lets selected creators upload horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes, and according to an exclusive Business Insider report, Meta pays some creators between $50,000 and $500,000 to post them. What Instagram still does not offer is what keeps creators on YouTube: a share of the ad revenue.

Instagram announced Features on Monday, October 26, 2026, in a long-form video by Tessa Lyons, Vice President of Product at Instagram, and in an interview that Head of Instagram Adam Mosseri gave to The Colin and Samir Show. Features are horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes, as long as a feature film, aimed at podcasts, vlogs, interviews and similar formats. They appear in the main feed and on the Explore page. According to TheWrap, the test started with creators in Brazil and rolls out to select creators in the US this month. Three days later, on October 29, Business Insider reported how Meta gets the first wave of content onto the platform: it pays for it.

I have to admit that I find this story more interesting than the format itself. A 90-minute upload limit is a spec. A $500,000 offer to a YouTuber is a strategy. Let’s take a closer look at both.

What Instagram has announced

Features are the core of the announcement. Creators in the test group can upload horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes, which is a clear break from the vertical, short-form logic that has defined Instagram since Reels took over. In his interview, Mosseri explained the change of direction with a simple statement: “We want to be the most culturally relevant platform, and to do that, we need to show up where people are.”

Three related tools come with the format:

  • Linked Reels: select creators can post Reels to their feed that link to a full Feature, so a short clip works as the entry point to the long video. In the Brazil test, up to eight clips can point to one long-form video.
  • Series: a dedicated place on a creator’s profile for episodic Reels. Series has been in testing for select creators in the US, India and Mexico since spring, and Instagram plans to expand it to more countries through the end of the year.
  • TV features: users can save Features and Series on their phone to watch later on TV, and Instagram is testing a “second screen” option that uses the phone as a remote.

The idea behind linked Reels is easy to read. Today, many viewers see a clip from a YouTube video as a Reel and then leave Instagram to watch the full video on YouTube. With Features, Instagram wants to keep both the short clip and the full video inside its own app.

$50,000 to $500,000 per creator

According to Business Insider, which spoke with people familiar with the deals, not every offer is equal. Meta has offered some creators $50,000 to post long-form video to Features, while others received six-figure offers, some of them as high as $500,000. Meta confirmed the program in general terms. “We’ve been public about the fact that we are funding Features content directly with some creators right now to support them,” a Meta spokesperson told the publication. “The details of those deals are confidential, but we’re excited to see the content going live.”

The most telling detail is what the deals do not require. Several people familiar with the agreements told Business Insider that there is no exclusivity to Instagram. One person said that Instagram asks creators to post any long-form video they publish on YouTube to Instagram on the same day. In other words, Instagram does not ask creators to leave YouTube. It asks them to bring their YouTube library along, in parallel (and I suspect a lot of YouTube executives read that sentence twice).

Reza Izad, co-CEO of the talent agency Underscore Talent, called the deals an “exciting opportunity” for creators. “Every time there’s a new feature in these apps that the company’s promoting, people will have more opportunity to be seen because there’s going to be algorithmic preference to this kind of content,” he told Business Insider. “And unlike short-form, there’s not a lot of abundance.”

He has a point. Early in a new format, there is little competition for the slot in the feed, and the platform has every reason to push it. My feeling is that this window will not stay open for long, but for the first creators, the reach could be considerable. That is a guess, though, because Instagram has not published anything about how Features are ranked.

We have seen this before: IGTV

Business Insider describes Features as the return of IGTV, and the comparison fits. Instagram launched IGTV in June 2018 with uploads of up to one hour, a standalone app and a vertical-video focus. In 2020, it added ads to IGTV and gave creators 55% of the ad revenue, the same split that YouTube uses for long-form video. In 2021, Instagram also funded long-form episodic shows from creators such as the “Sway Boys” and Nia Sioux. None of it gained traction. Instagram merged IGTV into a general “Instagram Video” tab in 2021 and closed the standalone app in 2022, as Reels became the company’s priority.

Paid deals are not new either. Last year, Meta paid creators thousands of dollars to post short-form videos to Instagram and Facebook, at a time when TikTok faced a possible ban in the US under a law that required its Chinese owner to sell the app’s US business. Instagram has also tested several bonus programs that paid creators for the performance of their Reels, but according to Business Insider, those programs have dwindled.

Mosseri himself has argued against long-form video on Instagram for years. In 2024, he said the platform would stay focused on short-form content, and in another interview that year he called Instagram’s earlier Reels bonus payments “burning money.” In the new interview, he admits that he opposed long-form video for a long time and now wants Instagram to lean into it. What is different this time: the format is horizontal, it is connected to a TV app, and it arrives after YouTube has proved that creator video works on the living room screen.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Colin and Samir (@colinandsamir)

The TV app is the real target

The long-form push is directly connected to the living room. Instagram first launched its TV app on Amazon Fire TV in the US in December 2025, then brought it to Samsung smart TVs and Google TV. Apple TV support is next; TheWrap reports a launch this month. The TV app now gives priority to Features, which makes sense: a 90-minute horizontal video is a TV product, not a phone product.

This is exactly where YouTube is strongest. As we reported in March, YouTube is now the world’s largest media company, and it has been the number one streaming service by watch time on US TVs for years. Instagram enters this space with a huge audience, but without a library of long-form content and without a long-form habit among its viewers. Seen from that angle, the checks are a way to buy a library quickly.

What about everyone else?

This is the big question that Business Insider also raises. A handful of creators get direct deals, but the rest of the creator community gets no platform income from Features at this time. According to Variety, Instagram does not plan an ad revenue sharing program like YouTube’s for these videos. An Instagram spokesperson said it is too early to share a long-term monetization model, and that the company is exploring brand, fan and performance-based incentives.

Creators raised the topic immediately after the announcement, and Mosseri answered in a post on X on Wednesday, October 28: “We understand the economics matter a ton, and are exploring multiple options to help long-form creators get paid.” That is a softer tone than in his interview, where he said that Instagram has no plans yet for a revenue share across short-form and long-form video. It is not a commitment, though.

What remains on Instagram today are its existing tools: brand partnerships, subscriptions, gifts from viewers, and invitation-only bonus programs. None of these pays a creator a fixed share of the ads that run next to their video. For a creator who uploads a 40-minute camera review or a behind-the-scenes documentary without a Meta deal, the direct platform income from that video is zero.

What YouTube pays in comparison

YouTube’s model is the benchmark. In the YouTube Partner Program, creators keep 55% of the ad revenue from their long-form videos, and YouTube says it has paid more than $100 billion to creators, artists and media companies in four years.

The bar to join is getting higher, though. As we explained in August, YouTube is changing its Partner Program rules from February 1, 2027. New channels then need 1,000 subscribers plus either 8,000 qualified watch hours in the last 365 days or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days, double the current requirement. Channels already in the program keep their status. YouTube also changed how it counts views in August.

So the trade-off is clear. YouTube makes it harder to enter its revenue program but pays a fixed share once you are in. Instagram is free to join and pays a few selected creators very well, but it pays everyone else no ad share on long-form video at all.

Could this start a bidding war for creators?

I think this is the most interesting long-term question. If Meta opens Features to all creators and adds an ad revenue share, YouTube would face real competition for long-form creators for the first time in years. Two platforms that compete for the same videos could push each other toward better terms, for example a higher ad share, lower entry thresholds, or more direct deals. Creators would be the winners of such a contest. To be clear, this is my speculation; neither company has announced anything in this direction.

History shows that YouTube does react. When IGTV launched in 2018, Business Insider reported that YouTube paid some top creators five- and six-figure sums so that they would not put new content on IGTV first. This time, the roles are reversed, with Meta writing the checks.

There is also a strong argument against a quick bidding war. In his interview with The Colin and Samir Show, Mosseri described Instagram’s performance-based payments to video creators as “ROI negative,” meaning they cost Meta more than they bring in, and said that long-form video needs a monetization model that does not lose money. A revenue share above YouTube’s 55% does not fit that statement. My guess is that Meta will first try to compete with reach, the TV app and selected deals, and only open a general revenue share if Features proves that it can bring in advertisers. I would be happy to be wrong about that.

Is Instagram a YouTube alternative for filmmakers?

As a replacement for YouTube income, no, not at this time. At CineD, we publish our long-form video on YouTube, and I don’t see a reason to move it while Instagram has no revenue model for the format. A channel that earns from long-form ads would simply lose that income.

As an addition, the picture is different, and this is precisely how Meta structures its deals: same-day uploads next to YouTube, not instead of it. Many creators already use Reels to promote their YouTube videos. With Features, that same short clip can lead to a full video that stays on Instagram. That is useful for creators whose income comes mostly from brand deals rather than platform ads, and for channels that are still below YouTube’s new 2027 thresholds and want to build an audience in parallel.

Several questions remain open:

  • When will Features be available to all creators, and in which countries?
  • Will Instagram add ads to Features, and if so, will creators get a share?
  • What upload specifications apply (resolution, frame rates, HDR, bit rate), and how does Instagram compress long-form uploads for TV playback?
  • Does Instagram give creators separate analytics for viewing on the TV app?

Instagram has not answered these questions yet. My guess is that the paid deals are a test as much as the format is: if the funded creators bring an audience, a broader monetization model becomes much easier to justify internally. If they don’t, Features could follow IGTV. But that is only my guess.

Availability

Features are in testing now with select creators in Brazil and the US. There is no public sign-up, no announced date for a general rollout, and no general monetization program for the format; only the creators with direct Meta deals get paid for now. The Instagram TV app is available on Amazon Fire TV, Samsung smart TVs and Google TV in the US, with Apple TV support next.

Would you post your long-form videos to Instagram on the same day as YouTube, with or without a check from Meta? Or does YouTube stay your only home for long-form? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: Nikon Raises Profit Forecast by 50% – but Cuts Its Camera Sales Plan for the Holiday Half
entry.summary: Nikon just raised its full-year profit forecast by 50%, and if you only read the headline number, that sounds like great news for a company that lost more than ¥100 billion last year. Look one level deeper, though, and the camera side of the story goes the other way: Nikon now ex
entry.content:
Nikon just raised its full-year profit forecast by 50%, and if you only read the headline number, that sounds like great news for a company that lost more than ¥100 billion last year. Look one level deeper, though, and the camera side of the story goes the other way: Nikon now expects ¥722 billion (about $4.66 billion) in revenue, ¥10 billion less than in August, and it says the cut comes mainly from a lower second-half sales plan for cameras and lenses. Here is what the numbers tell us, and what they don’t.

Nikon published the revised forecast on October 30, 2026, about a week before its full first-half results. Nikon’s fiscal year runs from April to March, so this covers April 2026 to March 2027. In August, Nikon was the odd one out of the earnings season, cutting its camera target on weak demand in China and rising memory prices, while Canon’s camera business was booming and CIPA’s first-half 2026 data showed a market that still grows in value. I was curious whether the second quarter would change that picture. Based on this notice, it doesn’t. (All dollar and euro figures here use Nikon’s own planning rates of ¥155 to the dollar and ¥180 to the euro.)

Where the extra profit comes from

The full-year operating profit forecast goes up from ¥11.0 billion to ¥16.5 billion (around $106 million / €92 million). Net profit for shareholders, which Nikon calls “profit attributable to owners of parent”, rises 60% to ¥16.0 billion (about $103 million / €89 million). Revenue goes the other way, down 1.4% to ¥722 billion.

Almost all of that improvement sits in the half that is already over. For April to September, Nikon had planned an operating loss of ¥5.5 billion; it now expects a profit of ¥9.0 billion. According to the company, three things did the work: higher service revenue in its semiconductor lithography business on strong chip demand, refunds of US import tariffs, and lower costs from spending cuts and postponed expenses. None of these has much to do with cameras.

The holiday half looks weaker

This is the part I find more interesting. If you subtract the first half from the full year, Nikon’s forecast for October to March drops from ¥396.0 billion to ¥387.5 billion in revenue, and from ¥16.5 billion to ¥7.5 billion in operating profit. So the full-year number only goes up because the first half beat the plan by so much. The second half, which includes the holiday season and is usually the strongest period for camera sales, now looks clearly worse than Nikon expected three months ago.

Nikon names the Imaging Products Business as the main reason for the lower revenue. The notice also lists which divisions get a higher profit outlook: Precision Equipment, Healthcare, and Industry. Imaging is not on that list, and I don’t think that is an accident. What the notice does not give us is the size of the imaging cut, because it contains no segment figures. Those should come with the full second-quarter results, which Nikon usually publishes in early November.

A lower bar was already set in August

It helps to remember where the imaging plan stood. In August, Nikon expected ¥290.0 billion (about $1.87 billion / €1.61 billion) in imaging revenue and ¥13.0 billion (around $84 million / €72 million) in operating profit, down from ¥17.2 billion a year earlier. It planned to sell 850,000 interchangeable lens cameras and 1.25 million lenses, and it cut its estimate for the whole interchangeable lens camera market by 300,000 units to 6.7 million. The reasons were China and memory costs, which we explained in our memory shortage overview.

Of that plan, ¥160 billion in revenue and ¥8.5 billion in operating profit were assigned to the second half. That is exactly the part Nikon is now revising down. My guess is that the camera unit target will drop again when the full results come out, but that is only a guess until Nikon publishes the figures.

For context, the group closed the last fiscal year with an operating loss of ¥112.4 billion (about $725 million / €624 million). Most of that came from the Digital Manufacturing Business, Nikon’s metal 3D printing division, which lost ¥106.2 billion on its own. Compared with that, any profit this year is a recovery for the group as a whole.

What about Nikon’s cinema push?

This is the question I care about most as a filmmaker, and the forecast can’t answer it. Nikon does not report RED or its cinema cameras separately, so the ZR, KOMODO, and V-RAPTOR all disappear into the imaging total. What we do know is the ambition: in its medium-term management plan from May, Nikon targets ¥360 billion in imaging revenue and ¥34 billion in imaging operating profit by the fiscal year ending March 2028, with a coming Z CINEMA series as part of that growth. A weaker plan for this holiday season moves those targets further away.

In my opinion, the best way for Nikon to change the camera numbers is new products and better support for the ones people already own. ZR owners are still waiting for that big firmware update (Nikon, if you are reading this: that would be a very cheap way to make a lot of filmmakers happy). And when Nikon, Canon, Sony, and Fujifilm executives spoke to Nikkei about the future of cameras, video was a central topic. We will follow up when the full first-half results and the revised imaging figures are out.

Nikon’s group profit is going up, but its camera business goes into the holiday season with a lower plan. Do you think the China slowdown and memory costs will change Nikon’s next launches or its prices? And are you waiting for Z CINEMA products before you buy into the system? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: Eurocine 2027 Dates Announced – Back at Budapest’s HUNGEXPO From April 29 to May 1
entry.summary: Eurocine returns to Budapest in 2027. The film and TV production show takes place from Thursday, April 29 to Saturday, May 1, 2027, at HUNGEXPO, which makes it one day longer than the two-day edition this year in May. The 2027 floorplan is already out, visitor registration is ope
entry.content:
Eurocine returns to Budapest in 2027. The film and TV production show takes place from Thursday, April 29 to Saturday, May 1, 2027, at HUNGEXPO, which makes it one day longer than the two-day edition this year in May. The 2027 floorplan is already out, visitor registration is open, and entry stays free.

Eurocine started in 2022 as Euro Cine Expo in Munich, organized by the team that also runs BSC Show in London. For 2026, the event moved from Munich to Budapest and changed its name to Eurocine. The first Budapest edition took place on May 8–9, 2026, at HUNGEXPO, with a symposium of more than 50 sessions that we previewed ahead of the show. According to the organizers, it brought together more than 150 exhibitors, with participants from almost 60 countries. By all accounts we’ve heard in person, they really liked the vibe and organization of the 2026 Budapest edition (also more than in Munich in the years prior to that), so they CineD team will consider going to Budapest next year.

The 2027 show is the sixth Eurocine edition overall and the second in Budapest. If you’d like to get a taste of what last year’s Eurocine was like, here is a recap:

What to expect at Eurocine 2027

Eurocine is built around four main elements: the expo, symposium, screenings, and the Eurocine Academy. The expo covers cameras, lenses, lighting, grip, aerial, virtual production, editing, and power, plus studios, locations, rental houses, and film funds. The symposium has talks, workshops, and panels on craft, industry practice, and new technology. Curated screenings of short films and documentaries are followed by Q&As with the filmmakers.

The symposium sessions are recorded and published on the free Eurocine Academy platform, so you can also watch talks from earlier editions there. Eurocine has not yet published the 2027 exhibitor list or the symposium program. According to the website, the exhibitor list will be announced soon.

Why Budapest?

The organizers describe Hungary as Central Europe’s production hub. On the Eurocine website, they list more than 30 sound stages, more than 50 production companies, and more than 20,000 industry employees in the country, together with a 30% film tax rebate. Hungary’s National Film Institute (NFI) supported the 2026 edition.

HUNGEXPO is Budapest’s congress and exhibition center at Albertirsai út 10. It has 75,000m² / 807,000 sq ft of event space in seven exhibition halls and a congress center. HUNGEXPO also offers dedicated filming studios and locations on site, alongside its exhibition and congress facilities.

Registration and exhibiting

Eurocine 2027 is free to attend and open to anyone with an interest in filmmaking, from students to established professionals. Visitors can register on the Eurocine website.

Companies that want to exhibit can see the 2027 floorplan now and register their interest in exhibiting with the organizers. For more information, please visit the Eurocine website.

Did you go to Eurocine in Budapest this year, or do you plan to go in 2027? Which manufacturers and topics do you want to see there? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Held Hostage by Vimeo – 18 Years of Uploads, Locked Behind a Paywall
entry.summary: In 2026, Vimeo started telling the world that storage on its individual plans is unlimited again. Read the fine print, and you’ll discover that “unlimited” covers only a video type almost no professional uses, and that long-time members aren’t even included. I opened my Vimeo acc
entry.content:
In 2026, Vimeo started telling the world that storage on its individual plans is unlimited again. Read the fine print, and you’ll discover that “unlimited” covers only a video type almost no professional uses, and that long-time members aren’t even included. I opened my Vimeo account in July 2008. Today, I can’t watch, embed, or download the videos I uploaded more than a decade ago unless I start paying. This is the story of how a free platform quietly turned our archives into leverage.

I joined Vimeo in July 2008. At the time, it was the obvious choice for anyone who cared about image quality. YouTube was still a low-resolution playground, while Vimeo had HD playback, a clean player, and a community of filmmakers who actually watched each other’s work. The Canon EOS 5D Mark II was about to change our industry, and Vimeo was where those first “cinematic” DSLR films lived.

Over the following years, I uploaded personal work, mostly (bad) short films, holiday trips, and skateboarding videos. After film school, it felt natural and logical to start uploading professional pieces on Vimeo: music videos, short films, wedding films, and plenty of early work. Some of these projects were made with almost no money, with friends and artists who trusted me with their image. They are a snapshot of where I come from as a filmmaker.

Eighteen years, one “Renew” button

A few weeks ago, I wanted to send a video I did a couple of years ago to a friend. To my surprise, my account now showed only six videos online. And that exact video wasn’t even among them.

So I logged in, and, oh, surprise.

So, according to Vimeo, my “Vimeo Plus membership expired,” which is why I “lost access to some of my videos.” That message even reassured me that getting everything back was “exceptionally easy. Just renew!”

There is just one small problem. I have never bought a Vimeo subscription. Not Plus, not Pro, not anything. I have never paid Vimeo a single cent. Yet I’m being asked to renew something I never purchased to get back videos I uploaded for free, under rules that didn’t exist when I uploaded them.

When I try to access my library today, a pop-up says I’ve reached the 5GB storage limit on my plan and invites me to “Join Vimeo Starter.” In practice, the minimum price to see my own work again is around €8 per month.

Back then, it was free, and nothing said “for now”

To understand why this feels like a betrayal, remember what Vimeo’s free account looked like when many of us joined.

The free tier, then called Vimeo Basic, was defined by a weekly upload allowance. In Vimeo’s own FAQ around 2014, the comparison table listed Basic storage as 500MB per week, and Plus as 5GB per week. As late as 2020, Vimeo’s pricing page still presented the free plan as 500MB per week, “up to 25GB a year.” The way they framed the limit told you how fast you could upload, not how much you could keep.

Nobody ever told us that our existing videos would one day count against a lifetime storage quota, and that crossing it would make them inaccessible. The implicit deal was simple: you bring the content, the community, and the traffic; Vimeo hosts your videos. That content is exactly what made Vimeo valuable. Staff Picks, the “Vimeo look,” the reputation of the platform among filmmakers- all of it was built on uploads from people like us.

Then the rules started changing. By 2019 at the latest, Basic accounts had a 5GB total storage cap, and members above that limit could no longer upload anything new. Vimeo justified it by the ongoing cost of storage and delivery. I stopped using Vimeo then and moved my work to YouTube, but it was okay, since my previous work was still online and I could still watch my password-protected or private videos.

Fine. Changing the conditions for new uploads is a business decision. But applying a new cap retroactively to videos uploaded years earlier, under completely different terms, and then locking them, is something else entirely. That’s not a pricing change. It’s like starting a game and changing the rules while you’re playing, or moving the goalposts after the match is over.

“Unlimited” until you read the fine print

Which brings us to 2026. Vimeo now explains that it has introduced “managed storage” on its individual plans. The headline and big announcement can sound generous: every new plan, including Free, comes with unlimited storage.

But the fine print says something different. According to Vimeo’s own help center, the unlimited part only applies to videos that are set to Public with embedding turned off. Everything else counts toward a capped “managed storage” allowance, including any video that can be embedded on another website, and any video that is Unlisted, password-protected, Embed only, or Private. In Vimeo’s words, managed storage covers the videos “where you control who can watch.”

As a filmmaker, it sounds like the platform built for us missed the entire point. Your portfolio embedded on your own website? Managed storage. A client cut behind a password? Managed storage. An unlisted link sent to a producer? Managed storage. The only truly unlimited content on Vimeo is public, non-embeddable video that people can only watch on Vimeo, which, in 2026, is precisely the use case nobody needs Vimeo for. YouTube does it for free, with an audience. If you’ve ever tried Vimeo’s search bar, I don’t need to elaborate much.

And even that generous partial “unlimited” isn’t for everyone. Vimeo specifies that older plans keep counting total storage, public videos included, and that the new managed storage figure only appears once an account transitions to one of the current plans. Long-time users on legacy accounts, like mine, are left on the old system: a hard 5GB cap that counts everything.

Three exits, all of them bad

So what happens to videos that don’t fit? Vimeo calls them “locked,” and the help center is very clear about what that means. Locked videos aren’t deleted, but nobody can play them, including through shared links and embeds. You can’t edit them. You can’t download them. Even worse, you can’t change them from Public to Private or turn off embedding to get them back.

That last point turns a storage policy into a hostage situation. Vimeo isn’t simply refusing to host more of my content for free. It is refusing to let me take my own files back.

Vimeo offers three ways to unlock videos.

#1: upgrade to a plan with enough storage. In my case, that means paying a monthly subscription to a platform I no longer use because of their past policies, for a 2TB plan, to retrieve a few gigabytes of videos uploaded more than twelve years ago. I’m not paying for storage. I’m paying for a key to my videos.

#2: make the locked videos Public with embedding turned off, so they no longer count toward managed storage. For personal content, that might be acceptable. For client work, NDA projects, unreleased cuts, or anything shared privately with the people in it, it simply isn’t an option. You don’t get to decide, alone, to publish a client’s wedding film to the entire internet to get it back. But that would also mean I could edit the status of some of my videos, which is not possible.

#3: delete videos until you’re under the limit. Vimeo notes that deleting a locked video is permanent: it doesn’t go to “Recently deleted.” In other words, you can free your archive by destroying it.

Pay, publish, or destroy. Those are the options. If that isn’t being held hostage, I don’t know what is.

Loyalty as a liability

What stings most is the asymmetry. A brand-new user signing up today gets the new managed storage system and an unlimited allowance for public videos. A member who joined decades ago, uploaded content when Vimeo needed it, and helped build the platform’s reputation gets a 5GB cap, locked videos, and a pop-up asking them to “renew” a subscription they never had.

In most industries, loyalty is rewarded. At Vimeo, the longer you’ve been there, the worse your deal gets.

This isn’t happening in a vacuum. As we covered in a previous post, “How Vimeo betrayed the Filmmakers Who Built It,” the platform spent years alienating its creator community through copyright purges, bandwidth caps, and a pivot to enterprise software, long before it was sold. Since then, Bending Spoons completed its $1.38 billion acquisition, laid off most of Vimeo’s staff, including the video engineering team, and went public on the Nasdaq with more than $4 billion in debt to service. A company under that kind of pressure doesn’t look at your decades-old free account and see a filmmaker. They see a cost line and a conversion opportunity.

Your archive is their leverage

The broader lesson goes beyond Vimeo. For many of us, video platforms quietly became our archives. We uploaded a project, deleted or lost the export over the years, and assumed the platform would always be there. That assumption was naive, but it was also encouraged. Platforms wanted our content, and “upload it and forget it” was part of the pitch.

The problem is that once your work lives on someone else’s servers, it stops being just your archive. It becomes their leverage. The more content you have, the older it is, the more emotionally and professionally valuable it becomes, and the more they can charge you to get it back. We’ve seen the same playbook elsewhere in the Bending Spoons portfolio: WeTransfer capped its free tier, and I, like many other filmmakers, stopped using it—and Evernote cut its free plan down to almost nothing. The tool you relied on for years becomes a toll booth.

To be fair…

Vimeo has legitimate arguments, and they deserve to be stated.

Storage and video delivery cost real money. I’m honest, they are not a charity, and they need to make money. Nobody is entitled to free hosting forever, and Vimeo has every right to charge for its service. Vimeo’s terms have also allowed the company, for years, to disable access to or delete content when an account exceeds its plan limits. A 2016 version of the terms already included that kind of clause for expired subscriptions. And yes, Vimeo was never meant to be a backup service. Any filmmaker who relied on it as their only copy, myself included, made a mistake. We could argue that these limits didn’t exist before 2010, but it’s an endless debate.

However, there’s a massive difference between refusing to store something and refusing to give it back. Vimeo could cap uploads. It could stop serving old videos publicly. It could even delete inactive content after a clear warning and a reasonable export window. Any of those would be defensible. What isn’t defensible is keeping the files, displaying their thumbnails under a “You’ve lost access to these videos” headline, and asking for a monthly payment to let you download them. That’s not a storage policy. That’s a ransom note with a nice illustration.

What now?

If you have an old Vimeo account, don’t wait for the next policy change to find out what you still have access to.

Log in and check your library, including the “locked” filter if your account has one. Download every video you can still access today in the highest available quality. Then apply the rule every one of us should already follow: keep at least three copies of anything that matters, on two different types of media, with one copy off-site. Local drives plus a cloud backup service is a nice option. In the end, a cloud backup service costs very little compared to paying a platform like Vimeo indefinitely to look at your own work.

For new projects, treat any hosting platform as a distribution tool, never as an archive. If you need client review, platforms like Frame.io or RevCut.io can work. If you’re looking for a creator-focused alternative to Vimeo, rushes that we covered here launched in 2026 partly in response to exactly this situation. Whatever you choose, keep the masters on your own drives.

The magic is gone

Vimeo’s pop-up notification was right about one thing: I’ve lost Vimeo’s magic. But not because a subscription I never bought has expired. I lost it when I realized the platform I helped fill with free content, back when it needed creators, now considers that content a debt I owe.

I’ll get my videos back, one way or another. What I won’t get back is the trust. And I suspect I’m not the only one.

Do you still have old videos on Vimeo? Have you received the same “renew“ notification, or been forced to pay to access your own work? Don’t hesitate to share your experience in the comments below!

entry.title: Nikon NIKKOR Z 120-300mm f/2.8 TC VR S Finalized – 420mm f/4 Reach, 6.5-Stop VR, and a Lighter Body
entry.summary: Five months after Nikon first announced development of the NIKKOR Z 120-300mm f/2.8 TC VR S, the finished lens is here, and the details left open in May are now filled in. The full-frame S-Line zoom combines a constant f/2.8 aperture with a built-in 1.4x teleconverter that turns
entry.content:
Five months after Nikon first announced development of the NIKKOR Z 120-300mm f/2.8 TC VR S, the finished lens is here, and the details left open in May are now filled in. The full-frame S-Line zoom combines a constant f/2.8 aperture with a built-in 1.4x teleconverter that turns it into a 168-420mm f/4 lens, internal zoom and focus, up to 6.5 stops of Synchro VR, and a new 2,735g (6.0lb) body.

We reported on the development announcement in May, when Nikon gave only the focal range, the aperture, and the teleconverter. At the time, weight, optical construction, autofocus motor, minimum focusing distance, stabilization performance, and pricing were still unknown. The finished lens now fills in those details. The lens follows the F-mount AF-S NIKKOR 120-300mm f/2.8E FL ED SR VR from 2020 as Nikon’s fast tele zoom. According to Nikon, the new Z version is about 515g / 18.16oz lighter than the F-mount lens, although the older lens has no built-in teleconverter.

The NIKKOR Z 120-300mm f/2.8 TC VR S is a Z mount lens for FX (full-frame) cameras, and it also covers DX. The optical design has 30 elements in 24 groups, with ED, Super ED, fluorite, SR (Short-Wavelength Refractive), and aspherical elements. The lens focuses with Nikon’s Silky Swift VCM (SSVCM) motor, zooms and focuses internally, and has an electromagnetic diaphragm with a range from f/2.8 to f/32. It measures approximately 128 x 353.5mm / 5.1 x 14in and weighs approximately 2,735g / 96.5oz. Nikon positions the lens primarily for sports photographers, citing figure skating, basketball, tennis, and soccer as examples of situations where fast action, changing subject distances, and different lighting conditions all come into play.

Two zooms in one barrel

The built-in 1.4x teleconverter first appeared in the Z lineup on the NIKKOR Z 400mm f/2.8 TC VR S in 2022. The 120-300mm is the first zoom in Nikon’s lineup to use the same idea. Nikon also calls it the world’s first interchangeable zoom lens with a constant f/2.8 maximum aperture and a built-in 1.4x teleconverter, based on its research as of October 29, 2026. With the converter engaged, the focal range becomes 168-420mm, and the maximum aperture drops by one stop to f/4. On an FX camera, the angle of view goes from 20° 20′ to 8° 10′ without the converter and from 14° 40′ to 5° 15′ with it. In DX crop mode, the lens reaches 3° 50′ at the long end with the converter.

Nikon says that the switch takes “a single action”, so there is no need to remove the lens or open the mount to an external converter. On the Z9 with firmware C:5.30 or later, the lens also supports a “Cycle image area using built-in TC” function.

Optics, coatings and focus

Nikon claims rendering “comparable to that of a prime lens across the entire frame” at all focal lengths. To control ghosting and flare, the lens uses the Meso Amorphous Coat, which Nikon describes as the best anti-reflection coating in its history, together with ARNEO Coat and Nano Crystal Coat. A fluorine coat on the front element repels water, dust, and grease.

Minimum focus distance changes with focal length. It is 0.98m / 3.22ft at 120mm, 1.38m / 4.53ft at 200mm, and 2m / 6.57ft at 300mm. Nikon does not give a maximum magnification figure. The A/M mode is Auto-Priority Manual, and Nikon has changed its sensitivity to reduce accidental switching to manual focus. A recall focus position function is available on cameras with current firmware.

What it offers for video

Nikon presents the lens as a sports stills tool, but some features are relevant for filmmakers who shoot sports, wildlife or events on Nikon Z bodies. The internal zoom and internal focus keep the length of the lens constant, so the balance on a support stays the same through the zoom range. Nikon also says the lens center of gravity sits closer to the camera body and remains consistent while zooming, which should make panning easier with a supported setup. The SSVCM drive sound is suppressed “to an almost-silent level”, which Nikon names as an advantage for video recording. Nikon gives no data on focus breathing.

The VR system gives up to 6.5 stops of correction (CIPA 2024, at 300mm without the converter) on a camera that supports Synchro VR, such as the Z6III that Nikon used for the measurement. Nikon says that this performance applies at the center and at the edges of the frame.

Build and handling

The barrel uses magnesium alloy and has dust- and drip-resistant sealing. The lens takes 112mm screw-on filters at the front and 46mm slip-in filters at the rear with the supplied holder. Nikon includes the HB-120 bayonet hood.

The tripod collar has a rubber cushion, an integrated finger grip, and a foot that fits Arca-Swiss clamps directly. Nikon recommends screw-type clamps only, because lever-type clamps may not hold the lens firmly. As with Nikon’s other recent super-telephoto lenses, the product page contains a warning that the magnets in the lens can affect pacemakers and other medical devices.

Price and availability

The NIKKOR Z 120-300mm f/2.8 TC VR S has a suggested retail price of $13,999.95 in the US, and it is available for pre-order at B&H. The lens is expected to ship in mid-November 2026. For more information, visit the Nikon website.

Is a built-in teleconverter worth this price for your sports or wildlife work, or would you rather carry a lighter zoom and an external converter? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Sony RIALTO 65 Announced – 65mm Camera Extension for VENICE 2, 9.6K Open Gate, 16-bit X-OCN
entry.summary: Sony’s RIALTO 65 is now official, and it puts a 65mm format sensor into a compact head that connects to an existing VENICE 2 body, on a cable or attached directly. It reads out 9.6K Open Gate, records 16-bit X-OCN internally, and arrives in the first half of 2027. I am at Sony’s
entry.content:
Sony’s RIALTO 65 is now official, and it puts a 65mm format sensor into a compact head that connects to an existing VENICE 2 body, on a cable or attached directly. It reads out 9.6K Open Gate, records 16-bit X-OCN internally, and arrives in the first half of 2027. I am at Sony’s event at Pinewood Studios today, where Sony is showing us the system.

When Sony announced the RIALTO 65 as a development project in June, we covered it with a long list of open questions about resolution, recording, and lens mounts. Today Sony answers most of them. The RIALTO 65 (model CBK-6510XS) uses a 53.75 x 35.83mm sensor with a 1.5:1 aspect ratio, about 2.2 times the area of full frame. According to Sony, it is among the largest sensors in any commercially available cinema camera. The head weighs about 1.5kg / 3.3lb, and it offers dual base ISO 2500 and 10000, with 15+ stops of latitude at ISO 2500.

This article is based on Sony’s press material. I will see the system at Pinewood today, and we will publish an interview video from the event in the next few days. So, for my own impressions, stay tuned.

A taller 65mm sensor

For me, the most interesting part is not the size but the shape. ARRI’s ALEXA 65 and the newer ALEXA 265 have had the digital 65mm market almost to themselves for years. Their sensor has a similar width, but a much wider aspect ratio of close to 2.1:1. Sony goes taller, to 1.5:1, which gives the proportions of a still photography frame.

That extra height is useful for anamorphic capture, for framing for different deliverables, and for reframing in post. At launch, there are two readout modes: 9.6K 1.5:1 Open Gate, which uses the full sensor, and 9.6K 2.20:1, with a diagonal of about 59mm, which suits more lenses. Sony says more readout modes will come with future VENICE 2 software updates. In my opinion, the 2.20:1 mode is the one many productions will use first. Many of the large-format lenses announced this year, such as the ZEISS Panoptes 65 primes and the Angénieux EZ 65 zooms, cover an image circle of about 60mm. That fits the 2.20:1 mode, but the full Open Gate needs glass made for true 65mm coverage.

Why the cable matters

The RIALTO name tells you how this works. As with the Rialto Extension System 2 and the VENICE 2 Extension System Mini, the head can move away from the body. In Extension Mode, a cable connects the two. It detaches at both ends, and Sony includes a 4.5m / 14.8ft cable, with a 12m / 39.4ft cable as an option. In Studio Mode, the head attaches directly to the body as one camera.

This is where I think Sony has a strong argument. Until now, digital 65mm meant a big camera. A 1.5kg head on a cable can go on a gimbal, into a car interior, or onto a handheld rig, while the body, media, and power stay somewhere else. The head also records tilt and roll as metadata for post.

Same VENICE 2 pipeline

The VENICE 2 body does the recording. So the RIALTO 65 writes to the same AXS cards, in the same 16-bit X-OCN, with S-Log3 and S-Gamut3 and the CineAlta color science that VENICE users know. For rental houses with VENICE 2 packages, this is the real selling point: the media, accessories, and post workflows stay the same. My feeling is that this is Sony’s main strategy here. It does not need to sell a new camera body, only a new front end for bodies that are already out there. That is my guess, of course.

What we do not know yet is how the sensor performs. Our VENICE 2 Lab Test gives a reference for the full-frame 8.6K version. Rolling shutter on a 9.6K sensor of this size is the first thing I want to see in our lab (Sony, if you are reading this, we are ready when you are).

Lenses, anamorphic, and ND

The RIALTO 65 has no lens mount of its own. Sony designed it for third-party lens mount adapters, so each production selects the mount for its lenses, including 65mm optics. With a lens and adapter that communicate with the camera, it records focal length, focus position, and aperture as metadata for editing, VFX, and virtual production.

This is a change from the Extension System Mini, which ships with E-mount and an ARRI PL adapter. It gives more freedom, but it also adds one more cost and one more decision for the camera team.
